intro: The Forlane has the lilting step of an old dance and chords full of sharp little surprises. Its dedication remembers Gabriel Deluc, a Basque painter killed in the First World War.

sections.label: A · A dotted dance in six
sections.mNote: Long–short figures dance over chromatic chords

sections.label: B · Detached chords and held notes
sections.mNote: The bass holds while the upper chords move

sections.label: C · Dotted figures and trills
sections.mNote: The dance’s short phrases sprout little ornaments

sections.label: Coda · Softly, at the same pace
sections.mNote: Sans ralentir: the last gestures keep the pulse

cues.title: A dance with sharp elbows
cues.text: Long–short figures give the 6/8 dance its lilt. The melody steps through chords crowded with sharps and naturals; even the quiet opening has a sting. Ravel marks it Allegretto, and lets the first little strain come round again.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, opening; Piano Practical Editions, bars 1–16, p. 18. The score has dotted figures, chromatic chord notes and a repeat after bar 8. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP560971-PMLP4975-Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A painter’s memorial
cues.text: Lieutenant Gabriel Deluc’s name stands above this dance. He is a Basque painter and a friend of Ravel, one of the men killed in the First World War whom Le Tombeau de Couperin remembers.
cues.evidence: The BnF records Deluc’s dedication and rank: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. His profession, friendship and death in the war are documented by Eric T. Williams, Kansas City Symphony programme, 5–7 April 2024, p. 6: https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf

cues.title: Couperin on Ravel’s desk
cues.text: Ravel prepares for his own Forlane by transcribing a forlane by François Couperin. The dance comes from northern Italy and finds a home at the French court around 1700. Ravel keeps its dotted step and repeated phrases, then fills them with his own wayward chords.
cues.evidence: Eric T. Williams describes Ravel’s Couperin transcription, the dance’s Italian origins and its French courtly history, Kansas City Symphony programme, 5–7 April 2024, pp. 6–7. https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf

cues.title: Chords against a held bass
cues.text: The piano alternates clipped chords with notes held across the beat. A bass note can keep sounding while the upper parts take another step. The two broad beats of 6/8 continue beneath these small disagreements.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, pp. 12–13: detached chordal writing, sustained lower voices and continuing 6/8 metre.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trills among the steps
cues.text: The later phrases keep the dance’s long–short rhythm and add trills and tiny grace notes. A trill briefly turns one note into a flutter; the phrase carries on underneath. The ornaments share the beat with the main notes.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, pp. 14–15, including the trill in the closing pages; the opening footnote specifies that grace notes fall on the beat.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The dance keeps its pace
cues.text: The final gestures become small and widely spaced. Ravel writes sans ralentir — without slowing — over the last pianissimo chord. The dance stops with its pulse still intact.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, final bars; Piano Practical Editions, p. 26, preserves the final pp and sans ralentir.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A small ending, without slowing
transitions.to: Coda · Softly, at the same pace
transitions.how: The piano breaks the dance into short phrases, rests and sustained notes. A last grace-note figure leads to a soft chord over a low E. Ravel marks the ending pianissimo and sans ralentir, keeping the 6/8 step right to the close.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Forlane, p. 15; Piano Practical Editions, final bars, p. 26.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
